German likes its compound words, as we're going to find out! English is a bit more variable as to whether it writes compounds as one word or two.

hints.hint: "Meer" and French "mer" have the same meaning.

subLevels.reveal: English still retains "mere" in some place names like "Windermere", the largest lake in England.

hints.alt: Image of a water fountain, with the words "Trinkwasser" and "Drinking water" on its sign

subLevels.reveal: Indeed, the excess salt in seawater would dehydrate you more than drinking nothing at all.

subLevels.german: Wasser, Wasser überall, und nicht ein Tropfen zu trinken.

hints.hint: The lament of the Ancient Mariner

subLevels.reveal: Coleridge's ballad actually says "Nor any drop to drink", but who quotes it like that? No one.

subLevels.german: Ich trinke Bier, du trinkst Milch.
Ich habe Kaffee, du hast Tee.

hints.hint: Since "du/thou" is just old-timey "you", "hast" is just old-timey...?

subLevels.reveal: Old English had "ic hæbbe" too, but English gradually smooshed together most present tense forms (except "has"!) while German kept alllll its verb distinctions.

hints.hint: Word order should be in natural English word order, not following the German, unless otherwise instructed.
Turn the "u" to an "i" to find a more familiar form.
"getrunken" is a past participle of a verb we've already seen a couple of times.

subLevels.reveal: This was not an easy one! Well done!

subLevels.german: Ich habe zu viel Bier getrunken.

hints.hint: There's no close cognate to "viel" in Modern English. It means "much".
The obvious consequence of the previous sentence.
